name: Alpenzoo Innsbruck
kurzbeschreibung: Alpenzoo Innsbruck on the slopes of the Nordkette is one of Europe's highest zoos, home to around 2,000 alpine animals across 150 species at 750 meters altitude.
beschreibung:
Overview

Alpenzoo Innsbruck, set on the sunny southern slope of the Nordkette mountain range below the Hungerburg at roughly 750 meters above sea level, is one of the highest-elevation zoos in Europe. Covering around 5 hectares of natural enclosure space, it provides a sanctuary for roughly 2,000 alpine animals from about 150 native species. The zoo is globally renowned for its thematic dedication to the wildlife of the European Alps, welcoming guests 365 days a year.

History & Conservation

Founded on September 22, 1962, by Austrian zoologist Hans Psenner, the zoo achieved global fame through pioneering breeding initiatives: in 1973/74, it accomplished the world's first successful captive breeding of the bearded vulture, laying the foundation for its reintroduction into the wild Alps. It is also deeply engaged in safeguarding the endangered northern bald ibis. Prominent residents include brown bears, wolves, lynx, alpine ibex, chamois, otters, and Europe's largest cold-water alpine aquarium featuring over 20 native fish species.

Visit & Getting There

Open daily all year round: summer 09:00–18:00, winter 09:00–17:00. Admission (2025/26 season): adults €16.00, children (6–17) €9.00, small children (4–5) €4.00, under 4 free. Popular combined ticket with the Hungerburgbahn funicular: adults €23.00, children €14.00. Public transport: take the modern Hungerburgbahn from Innsbruck Congress station to Alpenzoo station (5-minute walk over a suspension footbridge to the entrance), or take IVB city bus line W from Marktplatz directly to the ticket desk. By car: Weiherburggasse 37a (parking fee reduced at ticket office).

Tips

The zoo is set on steep hillside terrain with gradients up to 20%; free electric wheelchairs and the Bärenmobil shuttle are available for mobility-impaired visitors (advance booking recommended). To safeguard resident wildlife, dogs are strictly prohibited (licensed assistance dogs excepted). A winter visit is highly rewarding, as almost all alpine animals remain actively visible outdoors.
